claim: TKI-insensitive leukemia stem cells (LSCs) persist in most CML patients even after years of treatment.
source: Nonetheless, TKI-insensitive leukemia stem cells (LSCs) persist in most patients even after years of treatment and are imperative for disease progression as well as recurrence during treatment-free remission (TFR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about CML treatment outcomes.

claim: TKI-insensitive LSCs are imperative for disease progression in CML.
source: Nonetheless, TKI-insensitive leukemia stem cells (LSCs) persist in most patients even after years of treatment and are imperative for disease progression as well as recurrence during treatment-free remission (TFR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the role of LSCs.

claim: TKI-insensitive LSCs are imperative for recurrence during treatment-free remission.
source: Nonetheless, TKI-insensitive leukemia stem cells (LSCs) persist in most patients even after years of treatment and are imperative for disease progression as well as recurrence during treatment-free remission (TFR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the role of LSCs.

claim: Each CML patient harbored a unique composition of stem and progenitor cells at diagnosis.
source: Simultaneous measurement of global gene expression profiles together with >40 surface markers from the same cells revealed that each patient harbored a unique composition of stem and progenitor cells at diagnosis.
evidence: This finding is based on CITE-seq analysis of patient samples as described in the abstract.

claim: Patients with treatment failure after 12 months of therapy had a markedly higher abundance of molecularly defined primitive cells at diagnosis compared to optimal responders.
source: The patients with treatment failure after 12 months of therapy had a markedly higher abundance of molecularly defined primitive cells at diagnosis compared to the optimal responders.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study comparing patient groups retrospectively stratified by treatment response.

claim: The primitive fraction in CML patients is a mixture of molecularly distinct BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1- HSCs in variable ratio across patients.
source: The multiomic feature landscape enabled visualization of the primitive fraction as a mixture of molecularly distinct BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1-hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in variable ratio across patients, and guided their prospective isolation by a combination of CD26 and CD35 cell surface markers.
evidence: This finding is based on the multiomic analysis performed in the study.

claim: BCR::ABL1+ LSCs can be distinctly separated as CD26+CD35-.
source: We for the first time show that BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1- HSCs can be distinctly separated as CD26+CD35- and CD26-CD35+, respectively.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the study based on CITE-seq and validation experiments.

claim: BCR::ABL1- HSCs can be distinctly separated as CD26-CD35+.
source: We for the first time show that BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1- HSCs can be distinctly separated as CD26+CD35- and CD26-CD35+, respectively.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the study based on CITE-seq and validation experiments.

claim: The ratio of LSC/HSC is higher in patients with prospective treatment failure compared to optimal responders at diagnosis.
source: In addition, we found the ratio of LSC/HSC to be higher in patients with prospective treatment failure compared to optimal responders, at diagnosis as well as following 3 months of TKI therapy.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of patient samples at diagnosis.

claim: The ratio of LSC/HSC is higher in patients with prospective treatment failure compared to optimal responders following 3 months of TKI therapy.
source: In addition, we found the ratio of LSC/HSC to be higher in patients with prospective treatment failure compared to optimal responders, at diagnosis as well as following 3 months of TKI therapy.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of patient samples after 3 months of treatment.

claim: The acquisition of BCR::ABL1 kinase domain mutations within LSCs could necessitate a switch to another TKI.
source: For example, the acquisition of the BCR::ABL1 kinase domain (KD), and additional somatic mutations within LSCs could either necessitate a switch to another TKI or precipitate a blast crisis (Bolton-Gillespie et al., 2013; Giustacchini et al., 2017; Nieborowska-Skorska et al., 2012; O'Hare et al., 2007; Sorel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The acquisition of BCR::ABL1 kinase domain mutations within LSCs could precipitate a blast crisis.
source: For example, the acquisition of the BCR::ABL1 kinase domain (KD), and additional somatic mutations within LSCs could either necessitate a switch to another TKI or precipitate a blast crisis (Bolton-Gillespie et al., 2013; Giustacchini et al., 2017; Nieborowska-Skorska et al., 2012; O'Hare et al., 2007; Sorel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The LSC burden at diagnosis is linked to cytogenetic and molecular response in the chronic phase.
source: Moreover, even in the absence of KD mutations, the LSC burden at diagnosis is linked to cytogenetic and molecular response in the chronic phase (Khorashad et al., 2006; Mustjoki et al., 2013), and their presence is associated with recurrence during TFR (Pagani et al., 2020), thus compelling life-long treatment in the majority of patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The presence of LSCs is associated with recurrence during TFR.
source: Moreover, even in the absence of KD mutations, the LSC burden at diagnosis is linked to cytogenetic and molecular response in the chronic phase (Khorashad et al., 2006; Mustjoki et al., 2013), and their presence is associated with recurrence during TFR (Pagani et al., 2020), thus compelling life-long treatment in the majority of patients.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pagani et al., 2020.

claim: BCR::ABL1 transcript/gDNA quantification using qPCR, Sanger, and/or Next Generation Sequencing only captures cells positive for BCR::ABL1 expression and translocation.
source: The de facto standard for disease monitoring, BCR::ABL1 transcript/gDNA quantification using qPCR, Sanger, and/or Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), however, predictably only captures cells positive for BCR::ABL1 expression and translocation and does not inform the number and identity of fully leukemogenic cells (Radich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current monitoring methods with citation support.

claim: BCR::ABL1 transcript/gDNA quantification does not inform the number and identity of fully leukemogenic cells.
source: The de facto standard for disease monitoring, BCR::ABL1 transcript/gDNA quantification using qPCR, Sanger, and/or Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), however, predictably only captures cells positive for BCR::ABL1 expression and translocation and does not inform the number and identity of fully leukemogenic cells (Radich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current monitoring methods with citation support.

claim: The presence of BCR::ABL1 signal in the stem cell compartment rather than the lymphocytes correlates with TFR loss.
source: This is pertinent given that a combination of cell sorting and BCR::ABL1 quantification suggested that the presence of BCR::ABL1 signal in the stem cell compartment rather than the lymphocytes correlates with TFR loss (Kinstrie et al., 2020; Pagani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In remission, CML patients in chronic phase restore Philadelphia chromosome-negative (Ph-) hematopoiesis.
source: Using HSC specific markers, however, is confounded by the observations that in remission, patients in chronic phase restore Philadelphia chromosome-negative (Ph-) hematopoiesis (Bergamaschi et al., 1994; Carella et al., 1993; Claxton et al., 1992; Coulombel et al., 1983; Deininger, 2003), implying the co-existence of BCR::ABL1- HSCs and BCR::ABL1+ LSCs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The proportion of BCR::ABL1- HSCs and BCR::ABL1+ LSCs varies across individuals and treatment stages.
source: However, because their proportion varies across individuals and treatment stages (Mustjoki et al., 2013), and both LSCs and HSCs reside within similar immunophenotypic compartments (Lin-CD34+CD38-/low) (Eisterer et al., 2005; Petzer et al., 1996), discrimination between these populations – and thereby reliably estimating LSCs – remains difficult.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both LSCs and HSCs reside within similar immunophenotypic compartments (Lin-CD34+CD38-/low).
source: However, because their proportion varies across individuals and treatment stages (Mustjoki et al., 2013), and both LSCs and HSCs reside within similar immunophenotypic compartments (Lin-CD34+CD38-/low) (Eisterer et al., 2005; Petzer et al., 1996), discrimination between these populations – and thereby reliably estimating LSCs – remains difficult.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At diagnosis, Lin-CD34+CD38-/low BCR::ABL1+ cells could be divided into seven molecularly distinct subpopulations.
source: This demonstrated that at diagnosis, Lin-CD34+CD38-/low BCR::ABL1+ cells could be divided into seven molecularly distinct subpopulations, each reflecting unique lineage and cell state signatures.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work (Warfvinge et al., 2017).

claim: The proportions of BCR::ABL1+ LSC subpopulations changed dynamically upon therapy.
source: Importantly, the proportions of BCR::ABL1+ LSC subpopulations changed dynamically upon therapy and only a few surface markers efficiently discriminated between BCR::ABL1+ vs. BCR::ABL1- cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work (Warfvinge et al., 2017).

claim: CD26 was more frequently detected in the subpopulation most persistent during TKI treatment.
source: Of these, despite being generally reduced in BCR::ABL1+ cells upon therapy, CD26 was more frequently detected in the subpopulation most persistent during TKI treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work (Warfvinge et al., 2017).

claim: BCR::ABL1+Lin-CD34+CD38-/lowCD45RA-cKIT-CD26+ cells are the most TKI-insensitive cells.
source: The substantial treatment-induced changes observed within the stem cell population suggested that BCR::ABL1+ LSCs are themselves heterogeneous in terms of sensitivity to TKIs allowing us to define BCR::ABL1+Lin-CD34+CD38-/lowCD45RA-cKIT-CD26+ as the most TKI-insensitive cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work (Warfvinge et al., 2017).

claim: BCR::ABL1+Lin-CD34+CD38-/lowCD45RA-cKIT-CD26+ cells are strikingly enriched after TKI therapy.
source: Apart from being detected at diagnosis, these cells are strikingly enriched after TKI therapy (Warfvinge et al., 2017), a finding since confirmed in a transgenic mouse model (Shah et al., 2023), and in clinical observations documenting the long-term persistence of CD26+ cells in CML patients (Pacelli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: CD26+ cells persist long-term in CML patients.
source: Apart from being detected at diagnosis, these cells are strikingly enriched after TKI therapy (Warfvinge et al., 2017), a finding since confirmed in a transgenic mouse model (Shah et al., 2023), and in clinical observations documenting the long-term persistence of CD26+ cells in CML patients (Pacelli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pacelli et al., 2023.

claim: CITE-seq was used to quantify global gene expression profiles and highly multiplexed cell-surface protein profiles simultaneously within the same cells from nine CML patients.
source: Therefore, we used cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq Stoeckius et al., 2017) to quantify the global gene expression program, and highly multiplexed cell-surface protein profile simultaneously within the same cells from nine CML patients.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The CITE-seq analysis included >40 surface markers.
source: The CITE-seq analysis combines single-cell RNA-seq with simultaneous staining for a panel of >40 antibodies conjugated to uniquely barcoded oligonucleotides (henceforth Antibody derived tags, ADTs) aimed to cover the spectrum of normal hematopoietic stem (CD34+CD38-/low fraction) and lineage progenitors (CD34+ enriched fraction, HSPCs) as well as surface markers reported to enrich for CML stem cells (Herrmann et al., 2014; Järås et al., 2010; Kinstrie et al., 2020; Landberg et al., 2018; Sadovnik et al., 2016; Warfvinge et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Scarf projection was used to map each individual CML cell to a Lin-CD34+ healthy bone marrow reference.
source: To allow for accurate specification of LSPC heterogeneity without confounding effects generated from cell-type-irrelevant transcriptional signals related to BCR-ABL transformation per se, or inter-patient variability due to batch effects, we used Scarf projection (Dhapola et al., 2022) to map each individual CML cell to a Lin-CD34+ healthy bone marrow reference with a predefined heterogeneity.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: The normal reference consisted of 4696 Lin-CD34+ cells from two age-matched healthy donors.
source: To build a normal reference, we used our recently described CITE-seq profiles of Lin-CD34+ cells from normal BM from two age-matched healthy donors (henceforth, nBM) (Sommarin et al., 2021). The normal reference of 4696 Lin-CD34+ cells was visualized in a Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP, Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the reference dataset used in the study.

claim: Eleven cell clusters were identified in the normal bone marrow reference consisting of primitive cells, lineage progenitors and cycling cells.
source: We identified eleven cell clusters consisting of primitive cells, lineage progenitors and cycling cells in the UMAP, with near-to-equal distribution across the two nBM samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the normal bone marrow reference, supported by Figure 1B and supplementary figure.

claim: 14,274 Lin-CD34+ cells from nine CML patients were analyzed by CITE-seq.
source: Following CITE-seq of 14,274 Lin-CD34+ cells from nine CML patients, the cells were projected onto the nBM reference and annotated by label-transfer.
evidence: This describes the dataset analyzed in the study.

claim: CML patients, in general, were enriched for basophil/mast cell, MEP, MkP clusters and depleted for primitive, MPP1, 2, and ly/pDC/Mono clusters compared to normal bone marrow.
source: A comparison of abundance of clusters showed that CML patients, in general, were enriched for basophil/mast cell, MEP, MkP clusters and depleted for primitive, MPP1, 2, and ly/pDC/Mono clusters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing CML patients to normal bone marrow, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: A set of 71 genes comprised a pan-CML signature shared among all cluster comparisons.
source: In contrast, when considering genes differentially expressed in CML relative to nBM, and crucially shared among all the cluster comparisons, we identified a set of 71 genes that comprised a pan-cml signature.
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 50 genes were found to be consistently up-regulated in CML stem and progenitors.
source: Of the 71 genes, 50 genes were found to be consistently up-regulated in CML stem and progenitors.
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 21 genes were specifically and consistently upregulated in all clusters across nBM versus CML.
source: The analysis also identified 21 genes specifically and consistently upregulated in all clusters across nBM versus CML, and among others included DPY30 gene implicated in the maintenance of adult HSCs (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: All clusters from the normal bone marrow reference samples were represented in each CML patient.
source: By enumerating the proportion of molecularly defined clusters of individual patients, we found that all clusters from the normal bone marrow reference samples were represented in each patient.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis of individual patients.

claim: There was remarkable heterogeneity between patients in terms of relative abundance of constituent clusters.
source: However, there was remarkable heterogeneity between patients in terms of relative abundance of constituent clusters (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis of individual patients, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment failure cases displayed a higher abundance of the molecularly defined primitive cluster compared to optimal responders at diagnosis.
source: A focused comparison between optimal responders (CML 1–4) and treatment failure cases (CML 8–9) showed distinctive enrichment of specific cell clusters (Figure 3B), where failure cases displayed a higher abundance of the molecularly defined primitive cluster, multipotent progenitors 1 and 2, and myelo-lymphoid (My/Ly) and Ly/pDC/monocyte clusters at diagnosis.
evidence: This is a key finding comparing treatment outcomes, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment failure cases displayed a fourfold higher abundance of primitive cells compared to optimal responders at diagnosis.
source: Among others, the most conspicuous changes between optimal responders and treatment failures were observed in the primitive cluster (fourfold higher in failures), and MEP and erythroid cluster (∼threefold higher in optimal).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparing treatment outcomes.

claim: Optimal responders had approximately threefold higher abundance of MEP and erythroid clusters compared to treatment failures at diagnosis.
source: Among others, the most conspicuous changes between optimal responders and treatment failures were observed in the primitive cluster (fourfold higher in failures), and MEP and erythroid cluster (∼threefold higher in optimal).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparing treatment outcomes.

claim: Deconvolution of an independent bulk gene expression dataset from 59 CML patients showed a >threefold statistically significant enrichment of primitive cells in non-responders compared to responders.
source: The deconvolution results demonstrated a heterogeneous cell composition across patients, and overall comparison of imatinib non-responders (n=18 out of 59) versus responders (n=41 out of 59) showed a >threefold statistically significant enrichment of primitive cells in non-responders (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from computational deconvolution of an independent dataset, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Primitive cells were rarely detected in peripheral blood in contrast to the bone marrow.
source: Notably, the primitive cells were rarely detected in peripheral blood in contrast to the bone marrow, confirming the notion that cell type fractions differ in different tissues (Figure 3D), and the bone marrow is predictably a more reliable and abundant source of true primitive cells in CML.
evidence: This is a finding from the deconvolution analysis comparing bone marrow and peripheral blood.

claim: CD25, CD26, and CD93 could only capture a fraction of the primitive cells.
source: Interestingly, according to the ADT data, the established CML stem cell markers CD25, CD26, and CD93 could only capture a fraction of the primitive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing ADT expression in primitive cells.

claim: 6779 cells from the Lin-CD34+CD38-/low compartment from 8 CML patients were analyzed by CITE-seq.
source: To further investigate the molecular and immunophenotypic heterogeneity within the primitive cluster we performed CITE-seq on the stem cell enriched Lin-CD34+CD38-/low compartment from the same patients (n=8; 6779 cells Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the dataset analyzed for the stem cell enriched fraction.

claim: BCR::ABL1+ and BCR::ABL1- primitive cells were distinctly and consistently separated in the UMAP for each patient.
source: Remarkably, subsequent matching of BCR::ABL1+ and BCR::ABL1- cell IDs to the primitive cells in the joint Lin-CD34+ and Lin-CD34+CD38-/low UMAPs (indicated by red and black cell color, respectively), indeed revealed that BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1- HSCs were distinctly and consistently separated in the UMAP for each patient (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the multiomic analysis, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: BCR::ABL1+ LSCs in all patients were positioned immediately juxtaposing the downstream progenitor populations forming a continuum of differentiation hierarchy.
source: BCR::ABL1+ LSCs in all patients were positioned immediately juxtaposing the downstream progenitor populations forming a continuum of differentiation hierarchy characteristically observed in single-cell analysis of HSPCs (Pellin et al., 2019; Safi et al., 2022; Velten et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the UMAP analysis with citation support for the expected pattern.

claim: BCR::ABL1- HSCs formed an isolated and distinct cluster clearly detached from the rest of the cells in the majority of patients.
source: In contrast, BCR::ABL1- HSCs formed an isolated and distinct cluster clearly detached from the rest of the cells in the majority of patients, indicating that during the chronic phase of CML, active hematopoiesis is dominated by the BCR::ABL1+ LSCs while BCR::ABL1- HSCs reside in the bone marrow albeit in an inactive state with reduced contribution to hematopoiesis as previously suggested (Chen et al., 2023; Coulombel et al., 1983).
evidence: This is a finding from the UMAP analysis with interpretation supported by citations.

claim: CD26, CD25, and CD93 displayed a 2–8 fold elevated expression in BCR::ABL1+ primitive cells compared to BCR::ABL1-.
source: Moreover, using the ADT data we could validate the molecularly defined BCR::ABL1+ LSCs also by surface expression, with CD26, CD25, and CD93 displaying a 2–8 fold elevated expression in BCR::ABL1+ primitive cells as compared to BCR::ABL1-.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ADT analysis.

claim: 244 genes were specifically upregulated in BCR::ABL1+ primitive cells.
source: To gain an understanding of the nature of molecular program of BCR::ABL1+ vs. BCR::ABL1- primitive cells, we analyzed differentially expressed genes between the pooled primitive BCR::ABL1+ and BCR::ABL1- populations from all CML patients. This identified 244 genes specifically upregulated in BCR::ABL1+ and 180 genes upregulated in BCR::ABL1- cells (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: 180 genes were upregulated in BCR::ABL1- primitive cells.
source: To gain an understanding of the nature of molecular program of BCR::ABL1+ vs. BCR::ABL1- primitive cells, we analyzed differentially expressed genes between the pooled primitive BCR::ABL1+ and BCR::ABL1- populations from all CML patients. This identified 244 genes specifically upregulated in BCR::ABL1+ and 180 genes upregulated in BCR::ABL1- cells (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: BCR::ABL1+ primitive cells showed upregulated expression of IL2RA (CD25), DPP4 (CD26), IL1RAP, and LEPR (CD295).
source: Interestingly, among genes up-regulated in BCR::ABL1+ primitive cells included the expression of established CML markers; IL2RA (CD25), DPP4 (CD26), and IL1RAP as well as LEPR (CD295) a receptor recently described as a novel marker for Lin-CD34+CD38-/low LSCs (Landberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis with citation support for LEPR.

claim: BCR::ABL1- cells displayed upregulated expression of CRHBP and CXCR4.
source: In contrast, BCR::ABL1- cells displayed an up-regulated expression of the stem cell-related gene CRHBP (Barbieri et al., 2022; He et al., 2005) as well as CXCR4 important for homing and maintenance of normal HSCs (Sugiyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis with citation support.

claim: 28 unique markers were significantly up-regulated for either BCR::ABL1+ or BCR::ABL1- primitive cells.
source: To specifically define the surface markers for their ability to capture BCR::ABL1+ vs. BCR::ABL1- primitive cells, we compared significantly up-regulated ADTs for either Lin-CD34+CD38-/low BCR::ABL1+ LSCs or BCR::ABL1- HSCs cells across patients and identified markers with consistent expression across the data set. We found 28 unique markers to be significantly up-regulated for either BCR::ABL1+ or BCR::ABL1- cells (black or red colored bars in Figure 4B, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from ADT analysis, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: 17 ADTs marked BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and were detected in at least one patient.
source: Of these 28 markers, 17 ADTs marked BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and were detected in at least one patient.
evidence: This is a finding from ADT analysis.

claim: CD26 and CD25 were explicit and consistent markers of BCR::ABL1+ LSCs throughout the entire cohort.
source: However, only CD26, and CD25 were explicit and consistent throughout the entire cohort.
evidence: This is a finding from ADT analysis across all patients.

claim: CD93 was present on BCR::ABL1+ LSCs in 7/8 patients.
source: CD93 was present on BCR::ABL1+ LSCs in 7/8 patients and other previously suggested LSC markers like CD33 and CD56 specifically labeled BCR::ABL1+ primitive cells in only a fraction of the patients.
evidence: This is a finding from ADT analysis across patients.

claim: 11 ADTs were specifically detected in BCR::ABL1- primitive cells from at least one patient.
source: In contrast, 11 ADTs were specifically detected in BCR::ABL1- primitive cells from at least one patient.
evidence: This is a finding from ADT analysis.

claim: CD35 with approximately fourfold elevated expression was the only marker found to be consistently specific for the BCR::ABL1- HSC population across all patients.
source: Interestingly, CD35 with ~fourfold elevated expression as compared to BCR::ABL1+ LSCs was the only marker found to be consistently specific for the BCR::ABL1- HSC population across all patients.
evidence: This is a key finding from ADT analysis across all patients.

claim: CD35 captures all HSCs in healthy human hematopoiesis.
source: Intriguingly, we recently showed that CD35 captures all HSCs in healthy human hematopoiesis and that stem cell activity as measured by xenotransplantation assays and epigenetic profiling is restricted to CD35+ HSCs (Sommarin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work with citation.

claim: Stem cell activity is restricted to CD35+ HSCs.
source: Intriguingly, we recently showed that CD35 captures all HSCs in healthy human hematopoiesis and that stem cell activity as measured by xenotransplantation assays and epigenetic profiling is restricted to CD35+ HSCs (Sommarin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work with citation.

claim: CD26 showed the highest capture of the BCR::ABL1+ primitive cluster (>95%) with consistent capture percentage across patients.
source: CD26 showed the highest capture of the BCR::ABL1+ primitive cluster (>95%) with a consistent capture percentage across patients (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ADT gating analysis, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: CD25 captured >80% of the BCR::ABL1+ primitive cluster on average but displayed higher variability in capture efficiency compared to CD26 across patients.
source: This was followed by CD25 which captured >80% of the BCR::ABL1+ primitive cluster on average but displayed higher variability in capture efficiency compared to CD26 across patients.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ADT gating analysis.

claim: The CD35+ gate showed a specific capture of approximately 50% of the BCR::ABL1- primitive cluster.
source: In contrast, the CD35 + gate showed a remarkable specific capture of BCR::ABL1- primitive cluster (~50%) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ADT gating analysis, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: CD26+CD35- ADTs captured BCR::ABL1+ primitive LSC cluster at high purity.
source: Predictably, whereas a combination of CD26+CD35- ADTs captured BCR::ABL1+ primitive LSC cluster at high purity, the CD26-CD35+ combination marked BCR::ABL1- primitive HSC cluster with no contamination of BCR::ABL1+ LSCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from ADT combination gating analysis, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: CD26-CD35+ combination marked BCR::ABL1- primitive HSC cluster with no contamination of BCR::ABL1+ LSCs.
source: Predictably, whereas a combination of CD26+CD35- ADTs captured BCR::ABL1+ primitive LSC cluster at high purity, the CD26-CD35+ combination marked BCR::ABL1- primitive HSC cluster with no contamination of BCR::ABL1+ LSCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from ADT combination gating analysis, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: CD26+CD35- cells showed a strong signal for BCR::ABL1 expression by qPCR while CD26-CD35+ cells were BCR::ABL1low/negative.
source: The analysis showed a strong signal within CD26+CD35- cells for BCR::ABL1 expression while CD26-CD35+ cells were BCR::ABL1low/negative, validating the capacity of the combination of CD26 and CD35 to separate BCR::ABL1+ and BCR::ABL1- stem cells at diagnosis as well as after second generation TKI therapy.
evidence: This is a validation finding using qPCR, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Lin-CD34+CD38-/lowCD26+CD35- cells from CML patients at diagnosis displayed a strong signal for GAS2 by qPCR.
source: In addition, real-time qPCR analysis confirmed that Lin-CD34+CD38-/lowCD26+CD35- cells from CML patients at diagnosis displayed a strong signal for GAS2 (Figure 6B), one of the top genes from the CITE-seq BCR::ABL1+ LSC signature (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a validation finding using qPCR, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CD26+CD35- cells maintained GAS2 expression following 3 months of Bosutinib therapy.
source: Furthermore, CD26+CD35- cells maintained GAS2 expression following 3 months of Bosutinib therapy (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR analysis after treatment, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GAS2 has been linked to CML disease progression, cell cycle control, apoptosis, and response to Imatinib.
source: GAS2 has previously been linked to CML disease progression, cell cycle control, apoptosis, and response to Imatinib (Janssen et al., 2005; Radich et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LSC and HSC populations were indistinguishably deeply quiescent with average times to first division of 80–100 hr in culture.
source: However, LSC and HSC populations were indistinguishably deeply quiescent with average times to first division of 80–100 hr in culture (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–C).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro division kinetics experiments.

claim: There was no distinct difference in cell cycle status between BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1- HSCs.
source: Moreover, cell cycle analysis was performed by gating the corresponding cell populations in the Lin-CD34+CD38-/low CITE-seq data using ADTs. In accordance with the in vitro study, there was no distinct difference in cell cycle status between the populations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from cell cycle analysis of CITE-seq data.

claim: There was a substantially higher ratio of CD26+CD35- LSCs over CD26-CD35+ HSCs at diagnosis in prospective treatment failures compared to optimal responders.
source: Intriguingly, we noted a substantially higher ratio of CD26+CD35- LSCs over CD26-CD35+ HSCs at diagnosis in prospective treatment failures compared to the bone marrow of optimal responders, both using CITE-seq ADTs as well as in FACS analysis for CD26 and CD35 (Figure 6C–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a key finding comparing treatment outcomes, supported by Figure 6C-D.

claim: Following three months of TKI therapy, the percentage of BCR::ABL1+ CD26+CD35- cells decreased in both optimal responders and treatment failures.
source: Importantly, following three months of TKI therapy, the percentage of BCR::ABL1+ CD26+CD35- cells decreased in both groups of patients; however, there was a striking difference in the relative proportion of CD26+CD35- LSCs/CD26-CD35+ HSCs in both groups.
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis after treatment.

claim: The stem cell compartment of optimal responders was dominated by healthy HSCs at three months following treatment.
source: The stem cell compartment of optimal responders was dominated by healthy HSCs at three months following treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis after treatment.

claim: The stem cell population of failure patients still comprised of CD26+CD35- LSCs without re-establishment of HSCs at three months following treatment.
source: In contrast, the stem cell population of failure patients still comprised of CD26+CD35- LSCs without re-establishment of HSCs and restoration of normal hematopoiesis (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis after treatment, shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CML patients at diagnosis contain both BCR::ABL1+ LSCs and BCR::ABL1- HSC within the Lin-CD34+CD38-/low immunophenotypic compartment.
source: Moreover, longstanding observations have revealed that CML patients at diagnosis contain both BCR::ABL1+ LSCs vs. BCR::ABL1- HSC within the Lin-CD34+CD38-/low immunophenotypic compartment, and BCR::ABL1+ LSCs suppress residual normal HSCs (Chen et al., 2023; Coulombel et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BCR::ABL1+ LSCs suppress residual normal HSCs.
source: Moreover, longstanding observations have revealed that CML patients at diagnosis contain both BCR::ABL1+ LSCs vs. BCR::ABL1- HSC within the Lin-CD34+CD38-/low immunophenotypic compartment, and BCR::ABL1+ LSCs suppress residual normal HSCs (Chen et al., 2023; Coulombel et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A lower fraction of BCR::ABL1- normal stem cells at diagnosis and during therapy relates to hematological toxicity with delayed or compromised restoration of Ph-negative hematopoiesis upon successful response to TKIs.
source: Predictably, a lower fraction of BCR::ABL1- normal stem cells at diagnosis and during therapy relates to hematological toxicity with delayed or compromised restoration of Phneg hematopoiesis upon successful response to TKIs (Janssen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Prospective optimal responders to TKI treatment had a higher content of BCR::ABL1-CD26-CD35+ cells at diagnosis compared to treatment failures.
source: Prospective optimal responders to TKI treatment had a higher content of BCR::ABL1-CD26-CD35+ cells at diagnosis, and 3 months following therapy versus the treatment failures.
evidence: This is a finding from the study comparing treatment outcomes.

claim: Not all LSC subpopulations are equally sensitive to BCR::ABL1 inhibition.
source: Intriguingly, one of the emerging principles from the single-cell studies has been that not all LSC subpopulations are equally sensitive to BCR::ABL1 inhibition; while a majority of the LSCs are depleted, at least a fraction survives (Giustacchini et al., 2017; Warfvinge et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: There is an overall reduction in BCR::ABL1+ Lin-CD34+CD38-/low cells upon commencing TKI therapy.
source: This is corroborated by an overall reduction in BCR::ABL1+ Lin-CD34+CD38-/low cells but a striking enrichment of cKIT-CD26+ subpopulation displaying primitive and quiescent molecular program upon commencing TKI therapy (Warfvinge et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: There is a striking enrichment of cKIT-CD26+ subpopulation displaying primitive and quiescent molecular program upon commencing TKI therapy.
source: This is corroborated by an overall reduction in BCR::ABL1+ Lin-CD34+CD38-/low cells but a striking enrichment of cKIT-CD26+ subpopulation displaying primitive and quiescent molecular program upon commencing TKI therapy (Warfvinge et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Patients with activated immune signature at diagnosis are more likely to optimally respond to TKIs.
source: The observations that patients with activated immune signature at diagnosis are more likely to optimally respond to TKIs (Radich et al., 2023) serve as apt reminder for collective analyses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The pan-CML signature included CD81, a surface marker previously implicated in CML.
source: This included a constellation of genes such as surface markers, CD81 (Quagliano et al., 2020), nucleoside diphosphate kinase with transcriptional regulatory activity, NME2 (Kar et al., 2012; Thakur et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2014; Thakur et al., 2011; Tschiedel et al., 2012; Tschiedel et al., 2008; Yadav et al., 2014) previously implicated in CML, genes of histone family, and components of SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, BRD7 (Kaeser et al., 2008), as well as genes of histone methyltransferase family, KMT3A and 5 A (Husmann and Gozani, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis with citation support.

claim: CXCR4 is important for homing and maintenance of normal HSCs.
source: In contrast, BCR::ABL1- cells displayed an up-regulated expression of the stem cell-related gene CRHBP (Barbieri et al., 2022; He et al., 2005) as well as CXCR4 important for homing and maintenance of normal HSCs (Sugiyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CD62L was specifically present on BCR::ABL1- HSCs in 6/8 patients.
source: CD62L and CD10 were specifically present on BCR::ABL1- HSCs in 6/8 and 5/8 patients, respectively.

claim: The CD35+ gate captured approximately 50% of the BCR::ABL1- primitive cluster.
source: Interestingly, despite that relative expression of CD35+ was lower in the primitive cells compared to MEP/ERP cell clusters the CD35+ gate captured ~50% of the BCR::ABL1- primitive cluster.
evidence: This is a finding from ADT gating analysis.

claim: CD35 expression divided the CD26-, BCR::ABL1- primitive cells into one CD35+ and one CD35- fraction.
source: Interestingly, CD35 expression divided the CD26-, BCR::ABL1- primitive cells in one CD35 +and one CD35- fraction.

claim: All HSC activity in human BM immunophenotypic stem cells is captured within the CD35+ fraction.
source: This is in line with our recent observation that human BM immunophenotypic stem cells can be divided by CD35, where all HSC activity is captured within the CD35+ fraction (Sommarin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: CD26-CD35- captured BCR::ABL1- primitive cells likely representing non-leukemic MPPs downstream of normal CD26-CD35+ stem cells.

evidence: This is an interpretation based on the gating analysis and previous knowledge about HSC hierarchy.

source: Notably, only a minority of cells were positive for ADTs for the CD26+CD35+ combination as evidenced by an overall low capture of cells in general.
